case_info.scenario: A 69-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of progressive skin discoloration. His medical history included chronic kidney disease, chronic hepatitis C infection, cirrhosis, ischemic cardiomyopathy with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), and atrial fibrillation with prophylactic apixaban. He had recurrent staphylococcus bacteremia due to infection of an ICD lead and had been treated for the past 6 months with minocycline, 100 mg twice daily. His arms had been purple and bruise-like for several years but turned a near black color 1 month ago. He reported no discoloration of his sweat or urine. He had no history of malnutrition and reported infrequent alcohol use. Physical examination showed dense blue-black skin pigmentation of his forearms, dorsal hands, legs, and dorsal feet, as well as blue discoloration of his sclerae and teeth (Figure 1). He had normal-colored nails and oral mucosa. Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count of 15 800/μL (reference range, 4000-11 000/μL), hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL (reference, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), platelet count of 58 000/μL (reference, 150 000-400 000/μL), and INR of 1.8 (reference, 0.8-1.1). Complete metabolic panel showed increased creatinine (1.51 mg/dL; reference, 0.64-1.27 mg/dL) and elevated total bilirubin (1.7 mg/dL; reference range, 0.3-1.2 mg/dL). His estimated glomerular filtration rate was 40 mL/min/1.73 m2.
case_info.explanation: The keys to the correct diagnosis are the blue-black color of the pigmentation, the location on the distal extremities, and the involvement of sclerae and teeth. Potential etiologies for blue skin discoloration include drug-induced (eg, amiodarone, minocycline, hydroxychloroquine, and fluoroquinolones1), exposure to silver (argyria) or gold salts (chrysiasis), and deposition of pigmented fibers due to an inherited enzyme deficiency (endogenous ochronosis or alkaptonuria) or hydroquinone use (exogenous ochronosis).2Given this patient’s ongoing minocycline use, discontinuing minocycline is the best answer. This patient’s ecchymoses, most prominent at his proximal forearms, represent a distinct process from the blue-black pigmentation caused by minocycline. The ecchymoses were due to his use of apixaban, thrombocytopenia, bleeding diathesis, and skin fragility from age and sun exposure and would not necessitate stopping apixaban (choice A). Hemochromatosis (choice C) causes skin dyspigmentation that is typically diffuse and brown or slate-gray.3Pellagra, caused by deficiency in niacin (vitamin B3) (choice D), presents with a photodistributed rash; however, the rash is red or brown and does not discolor sclerae or teeth.2 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation presents as blue-hued pigmentation of the skin that may also involve the sclerae, nails, teeth, and oral mucosa. The reported incidence varies from 2% to 15% in patients treated for acne to 41% to 54% in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and orthopedic infections, respectively.4-6 Although minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation is a clinical diagnosis, skin biopsy can confirm the diagnosis and reveals subepidermal deposition of granular black pigment both interstitially and intracellularly (Figure 2). The pigment reacts positively with staining techniques used to detect iron and/or melanin (Perl’s Prussian blue and Fontana-Masson, respectively). In contrast, ecchymoses stain positive for iron only. While the mechanism of hyperpigmentation remains unclear, histopathologic studies indicate that minocycline and/or its metabolites likely form insoluble complexes with iron that deposit in tissue.7 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation is classified into 3 types based on clinical findings and histologic staining, though these categories may overlap. In type I, blue pigmentation is found in scars, commonly facial acne scars, and stains positive for iron only. In type II, blue pigmentation affects normal skin, typically on the extremities, and stains positive for both iron and melanin. Type III presents with muddy brown discoloration most prominent in sun-exposed skin and stains positive for melanin.8 This patient’s presentation was consistent with type II hyperpigmentation and notable for both the striking degree of pigmentation and for its rapid development after only 6 months of treatment. Most minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation occurs after a year, though small case series have reported pigmentation after only a few weeks.5,6,9Several characteristics of this patient may have contributed to the more rapid onset, including the longstanding purpura on his arms, which increases dermal iron available for chelation, as well as hepatic and kidney disease, which impair drug metabolism and excretion. Minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation persists after drug cessation and is challenging to treat. Given the small size of the pigment particle, treatment is best approached with picosecond or Q-switched lasers.10In addition to its effects on skin pigmentation, minocycline use in children can result in permanent teeth discoloration and bone hypoplasia and should be avoided during pregnancy and in children younger than 8 years old.2 Minocycline was discontinued and daptomycin was started in its place. The patient declined treatment for the pigmentation changes because they were not bothersome to him.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

His medical history included chronic kidney disease, chronic hepatitis C infection, cirrhosis, ischemic cardiomyopathy with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), and atrial fibrillation with prophylactic apixaban. Complete metabolic panel showed increased creatinine (1.51 mg/dL; reference, 0.64-1.27 mg/dL) and elevated total bilirubin (1.7 mg/dL; reference range, 0.3-1.2 mg/dL). [Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

His medical history included chronic kidney disease, chronic hepatitis C infection, cirrhosis, ischemic cardiomyopathy with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), and atrial fibrillation with prophylactic apixaban. He had recurrent staphylococcus bacteremia due to infection of an ICD lead and had been treated for the past 6 months with minocycline, 100 mg twice daily. Complete metabolic panel showed increased creatinine (1.51 mg/dL; reference, 0.64-1.27 mg/dL) and elevated total bilirubin (1.7 mg/dL; reference range, 0.3-1.2 mg/dL). His estimated glomerular filtration rate was 40 mL/min/1.73 m2.
case_info.explanation: The keys to the correct diagnosis are the blue-black color of the pigmentation, the location on the distal extremities, and the involvement of sclerae and teeth. Potential etiologies for blue skin discoloration include drug-induced (eg, amiodarone, minocycline, hydroxychloroquine, and fluoroquinolones1), exposure to silver (argyria) or gold salts (chrysiasis), and deposition of pigmented fibers due to an inherited enzyme deficiency (endogenous ochronosis or alkaptonuria) or hydroquinone use (exogenous ochronosis).2Given this patient’s ongoing minocycline use, discontinuing minocycline is the best answer. This patient’s ecchymoses, most prominent at his proximal forearms, represent a distinct process from the blue-black pigmentation caused by minocycline. The ecchymoses were due to his use of apixaban, thrombocytopenia, bleeding diathesis, and skin fragility from age and sun exposure and would not necessitate stopping apixaban (choice A). Hemochromatosis (choice C) causes skin dyspigmentation that is typically diffuse and brown or slate-gray.3Pellagra, caused by deficiency in niacin (vitamin B3) (choice D), presents with a photodistributed rash; however, the rash is red or brown and does not discolor sclerae or teeth.2 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation presents as blue-hued pigmentation of the skin that may also involve the sclerae, nails, teeth, and oral mucosa. The reported incidence varies from 2% to 15% in patients treated for acne to 41% to 54% in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and orthopedic infections, respectively.4-6 Although minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation is a clinical diagnosis, skin biopsy can confirm the diagnosis and reveals subepidermal deposition of granular black pigment both interstitially and intracellularly (Figure 2). The pigment reacts positively with staining techniques used to detect iron and/or melanin (Perl’s Prussian blue and Fontana-Masson, respectively). In contrast, ecchymoses stain positive for iron only. While the mechanism of hyperpigmentation remains unclear, histopathologic studies indicate that minocycline and/or its metabolites likely form insoluble complexes with iron that deposit in tissue.7 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation is classified into 3 types based on clinical findings and histologic staining, though these categories may overlap. In type I, blue pigmentation is found in scars, commonly facial acne scars, and stains positive for iron only. In type II, blue pigmentation affects normal skin, typically on the extremities, and stains positive for both iron and melanin. Type III presents with muddy brown discoloration most prominent in sun-exposed skin and stains positive for melanin.8 This patient’s presentation was consistent with type II hyperpigmentation and notable for both the striking degree of pigmentation and for its rapid development after only 6 months of treatment. Most minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation occurs after a year, though small case series have reported pigmentation after only a few weeks.5,6,9Several characteristics of this patient may have contributed to the more rapid onset, including the longstanding purpura on his arms, which increases dermal iron available for chelation, as well as hepatic and kidney disease, which impair drug metabolism and excretion. Minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation persists after drug cessation and is challenging to treat. Given the small size of the pigment particle, treatment is best approached with picosecond or Q-switched lasers.10In addition to its effects on skin pigmentation, minocycline use in children can result in permanent teeth discoloration and bone hypoplasia and should be avoided during pregnancy and in children younger than 8 years old.2 Minocycline was discontinued and daptomycin was started in its place. The patient declined treatment for the pigmentation changes because they were not bothersome to him.

case_info.explanation: The keys to the correct diagnosis are the blue-black color of the pigmentation, the location on the distal extremities, and the involvement of sclerae and teeth. Potential etiologies for blue skin discoloration include drug-induced (eg, amiodarone, minocycline, hydroxychloroquine, and fluoroquinolones1), exposure to silver (argyria) or gold salts (chrysiasis), and deposition of pigmented fibers due to an inherited enzyme deficiency (endogenous ochronosis or alkaptonuria) or hydroquinone use (exogenous ochronosis).2Given this patient’s ongoing minocycline use, discontinuing minocycline is the best answer. This patient’s ecchymoses, most prominent at his proximal forearms, represent a distinct process from the blue-black pigmentation caused by minocycline. The ecchymoses were due to his use of apixaban, thrombocytopenia, bleeding diathesis, and skin fragility from age and sun exposure and would not necessitate stopping apixaban (choice A). Hemochromatosis (choice C) causes skin dyspigmentation that is typically diffuse and brown or slate-gray.3Pellagra, caused by deficiency in niacin (vitamin B3) (choice D), presents with a photodistributed rash; however, the rash is red or brown and does not discolor sclerae or teeth.2 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation presents as blue-hued pigmentation of the skin that may also involve the sclerae, nails, teeth, and oral mucosa. The reported incidence varies from 2% to 15% in patients treated for acne to 41% to 54% in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and orthopedic infections, respectively.4-6 Although minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation is a clinical diagnosis, skin biopsy can confirm the diagnosis and reveals subepidermal deposition of granular black pigment both interstitially and intracellularly (Figure 2). The pigment reacts positively with staining techniques used to detect iron and/or melanin (Perl’s Prussian blue and Fontana-Masson, respectively). In contrast, ecchymoses stain positive for iron only. While the mechanism of hyperpigmentation remains unclear, histopathologic studies indicate that minocycline and/or its metabolites likely form insoluble complexes with iron that deposit in tissue.7 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation is classified into 3 types based on clinical findings and histologic staining, though these categories may overlap. In type I, blue pigmentation is found in scars, commonly facial acne scars, and stains positive for iron only. In type II, blue pigmentation affects normal skin, typically on the extremities, and stains positive for both iron and melanin. Type III presents with muddy brown discoloration most prominent in sun-exposed skin and stains positive for melanin.8 This patient’s presentation was consistent with type II hyperpigmentation and notable for both the striking degree of pigmentation and for its rapid development after only 6 months of treatment. Most minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation occurs after a year, though small case series have reported pigmentation after only a few weeks.5,6,9Several characteristics of this patient may have contributed to the more rapid onset, including the longstanding purpura on his arms, which increases dermal iron available for chelation, as well as hepatic and kidney disease, which impair drug metabolism and excretion. Minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation persists after drug cessation and is challenging to treat. Given the small size of the pigment particle, treatment is best approached with picosecond or Q-switched lasers.10In addition to its effects on skin pigmentation, minocycline use in children can result in permanent teeth discoloration and bone hypoplasia and should be avoided during pregnancy and in children younger than 8 years old.2 Minocycline was discontinued and daptomycin was started in its place. The patient declined treatment for the pigmentation changes because they were not bothersome to him.

A 69-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of progressive skin discoloration. His medical history included chronic kidney disease, chronic hepatitis C infection, cirrhosis, ischemic cardiomyopathy with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), and atrial fibrillation with prophylactic apixaban. He had recurrent staphylococcus bacteremia due to infection of an ICD lead and had been treated for the past 6 months with minocycline, 100 mg twice daily. His arms had been purple and bruise-like for several years but turned a near black color 1 month ago. He reported no discoloration of his sweat or urine. He had no history of malnutrition and reported infrequent alcohol use. Physical examination showed dense blue-black skin pigmentation of his forearms, dorsal hands, legs, and dorsal feet, as well as blue discoloration of his sclerae and teeth (Figure 1). He had normal-colored nails and oral mucosa. Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count of 15 800/μL (reference range, 4000-11 000/μL), hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL (reference, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), platelet count of 58 000/μL (reference, 150 000-400 000/μL), and INR of 1.8 (reference, 0.8-1.1). Complete metabolic panel showed increased creatinine (1.51 mg/dL; reference, 0.64-1.27 mg/dL) and elevated total bilirubin (1.7 mg/dL; reference range, 0.3-1.2 mg/dL). His estimated glomerular filtration rate was 40 mL/min/1.73 m2.

He had recurrent staphylococcus bacteremia due to infection of an ICD lead and had been treated for the past 6 months with minocycline, 100 mg twice daily. His arms had been purple and bruise-like for several years but turned a near black color 1 month ago. He reported no discoloration of his sweat or urine. He had no history of malnutrition and reported infrequent alcohol use. Physical examination showed dense blue-black skin pigmentation of his forearms, dorsal hands, legs, and dorsal feet, as well as blue discoloration of his sclerae and teeth (Figure 1). He had normal-colored nails and oral mucosa. Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count of 15 800/μL (reference range, 4000-11 000/μL), hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL (reference, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), platelet count of 58 000/μL (reference, 150 000-400 000/μL), and INR of 1.8 (reference, 0.8-1.1). Complete metabolic panel showed increased creatinine (1.51 mg/dL; reference, 0.64-1.27 mg/dL) and elevated total bilirubin (1.7 mg/dL; reference range, 0.3-1.2 mg/dL). His estimated glomerular filtration rate was 40 mL/min/1.73 m2.
case_info.explanation: The keys to the correct diagnosis are the blue-black color of the pigmentation, the location on the distal extremities, and the involvement of sclerae and teeth. Potential etiologies for blue skin discoloration include drug-induced (eg, amiodarone, minocycline, hydroxychloroquine, and fluoroquinolones1), exposure to silver (argyria) or gold salts (chrysiasis), and deposition of pigmented fibers due to an inherited enzyme deficiency (endogenous ochronosis or alkaptonuria) or hydroquinone use (exogenous ochronosis).2Given this patient’s ongoing minocycline use, discontinuing minocycline is the best answer. This patient’s ecchymoses, most prominent at his proximal forearms, represent a distinct process from the blue-black pigmentation caused by minocycline. The ecchymoses were due to his use of apixaban, thrombocytopenia, bleeding diathesis, and skin fragility from age and sun exposure and would not necessitate stopping apixaban (choice A). Hemochromatosis (choice C) causes skin dyspigmentation that is typically diffuse and brown or slate-gray.3Pellagra, caused by deficiency in niacin (vitamin B3) (choice D), presents with a photodistributed rash; however, the rash is red or brown and does not discolor sclerae or teeth.2 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation presents as blue-hued pigmentation of the skin that may also involve the sclerae, nails, teeth, and oral mucosa. The reported incidence varies from 2% to 15% in patients treated for acne to 41% to 54% in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and orthopedic infections, respectively.4-6 Although minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation is a clinical diagnosis, skin biopsy can confirm the diagnosis and reveals subepidermal deposition of granular black pigment both interstitially and intracellularly (Figure 2). The pigment reacts positively with staining techniques used to detect iron and/or melanin (Perl’s Prussian blue and Fontana-Masson, respectively). In contrast, ecchymoses stain positive for iron only. While the mechanism of hyperpigmentation remains unclear, histopathologic studies indicate that minocycline and/or its metabolites likely form insoluble complexes with iron that deposit in tissue.7 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation is classified into 3 types based on clinical findings and histologic staining, though these categories may overlap. In type I, blue pigmentation is found in scars, commonly facial acne scars, and stains positive for iron only. In type II, blue pigmentation affects normal skin, typically on the extremities, and stains positive for both iron and melanin. Type III presents with muddy brown discoloration most prominent in sun-exposed skin and stains positive for melanin.8 This patient’s presentation was consistent with type II hyperpigmentation and notable for both the striking degree of pigmentation and for its rapid development after only 6 months of treatment. Most minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation occurs after a year, though small case series have reported pigmentation after only a few weeks.5,6,9Several characteristics of this patient may have contributed to the more rapid onset, including the longstanding purpura on his arms, which increases dermal iron available for chelation, as well as hepatic and kidney disease, which impair drug metabolism and excretion. Minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation persists after drug cessation and is challenging to treat. Given the small size of the pigment particle, treatment is best approached with picosecond or Q-switched lasers.10In addition to its effects on skin pigmentation, minocycline use in children can result in permanent teeth discoloration and bone hypoplasia and should be avoided during pregnancy and in children younger than 8 years old.2 Minocycline was discontinued and daptomycin was started in its place. The patient declined treatment for the pigmentation changes because they were not bothersome to him.

You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal.

Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 9.5. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and

       findings."

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

2. Performance

       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

Potential etiologies for blue skin discoloration include drug-induced (eg, amiodarone, minocycline, hydroxychloroquine, and fluoroquinolones1), exposure to silver (argyria) or gold salts (chrysiasis), and deposition of pigmented fibers due to an inherited enzyme deficiency (endogenous ochronosis or alkaptonuria) or hydroquinone use (exogenous ochronosis).2Given this patient’s ongoing minocycline use, discontinuing minocycline is the best answer. This patient’s ecchymoses, most prominent at his proximal forearms, represent a distinct process from the blue-black pigmentation caused by minocycline. The ecchymoses were due to his use of apixaban, thrombocytopenia, bleeding diathesis, and skin fragility from age and sun exposure and would not necessitate stopping apixaban (choice A). Hemochromatosis (choice C) causes skin dyspigmentation that is typically diffuse and brown or slate-gray.3Pellagra, caused by deficiency in niacin (vitamin B3) (choice D), presents with a photodistributed rash; however, the rash is red or brown and does not discolor sclerae or teeth.2 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation presents as blue-hued pigmentation of the skin that may also involve the sclerae, nails, teeth, and oral mucosa. The reported incidence varies from 2% to 15% in patients treated for acne to 41% to 54% in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and orthopedic infections, respectively.4-6 Although minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation is a clinical diagnosis, skin biopsy can confirm the diagnosis and reveals subepidermal deposition of granular black pigment both interstitially and intracellularly (Figure 2). The pigment reacts positively with staining techniques used to detect iron and/or melanin (Perl’s Prussian blue and Fontana-Masson, respectively). In contrast, ecchymoses stain positive for iron only. While the mechanism of hyperpigmentation remains unclear, histopathologic studies indicate that minocycline and/or its metabolites likely form insoluble complexes with iron that deposit in tissue.7 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation is classified into 3 types based on clinical findings and histologic staining, though these categories may overlap. In type I, blue pigmentation is found in scars, commonly facial acne scars, and stains positive for iron only. In type II, blue pigmentation affects normal skin, typically on the extremities, and stains positive for both iron and melanin. Type III presents with muddy brown discoloration most prominent in sun-exposed skin and stains positive for melanin.8 This patient’s presentation was consistent with type II hyperpigmentation and notable for both the striking degree of pigmentation and for its rapid development after only 6 months of treatment. Most minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation occurs after a year, though small case series have reported pigmentation after only a few weeks.5,6,9Several characteristics of this patient may have contributed to the more rapid onset, including the longstanding purpura on his arms, which increases dermal iron available for chelation, as well as hepatic and kidney disease, which impair drug metabolism and excretion. Minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation persists after drug cessation and is challenging to treat. Given the small size of the pigment particle, treatment is best approached with picosecond or Q-switched lasers.10In addition to its effects on skin pigmentation, minocycline use in children can result in permanent teeth discoloration and bone hypoplasia and should be avoided during pregnancy and in children younger than 8 years old.2 Minocycline was discontinued and daptomycin was started in its place. The patient declined treatment for the pigmentation changes because they were not bothersome to him.

case_info.scenario: A 69-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of progressive skin discoloration. His medical history included chronic kidney disease, chronic hepatitis C infection, cirrhosis, ischemic cardiomyopathy with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), and atrial fibrillation with prophylactic apixaban. He had recurrent staphylococcus bacteremia due to infection of an ICD lead and had been treated for the past 6 months with minocycline, 100 mg twice daily. His arms had been purple and bruise-like for several years but turned a near black color 1 month ago. He reported no discoloration of his sweat or urine. He had no history of malnutrition and reported infrequent alcohol use. Physical examination showed dense blue-black skin pigmentation of his forearms, dorsal hands, legs, and dorsal feet, as well as blue discoloration of his sclerae and teeth (Figure 1). He had normal-colored nails and oral mucosa. Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count of 15 800/μL (reference range, 4000-11 000/μL), hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL (reference, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), platelet count of 58 000/μL (reference, 150 000-400 000/μL), and INR of 1.8 (reference, 0.8-1.1). Complete metabolic panel showed increased creatinine (1.51 mg/dL; reference, 0.64-1.27 mg/dL) and elevated total bilirubin (1.7 mg/dL; reference range, 0.3-1.2 mg/dL). His estimated glomerular filtration rate was 40 mL/min/1.73 m2.
case_info.explanation: The keys to the correct diagnosis are the blue-black color of the pigmentation, the location on the distal extremities, and the involvement of sclerae and teeth. Potential etiologies for blue skin discoloration include drug-induced (eg, amiodarone, minocycline, hydroxychloroquine, and fluoroquinolones1), exposure to silver (argyria) or gold salts (chrysiasis), and deposition of pigmented fibers due to an inherited enzyme deficiency (endogenous ochronosis or alkaptonuria) or hydroquinone use (exogenous ochronosis).2Given this patient’s ongoing minocycline use, discontinuing minocycline is the best answer. This patient’s ecchymoses, most prominent at his proximal forearms, represent a distinct process from the blue-black pigmentation caused by minocycline. The ecchymoses were due to his use of apixaban, thrombocytopenia, bleeding diathesis, and skin fragility from age and sun exposure and would not necessitate stopping apixaban (choice A). Hemochromatosis (choice C) causes skin dyspigmentation that is typically diffuse and brown or slate-gray.3Pellagra, caused by deficiency in niacin (vitamin B3) (choice D), presents with a photodistributed rash; however, the rash is red or brown and does not discolor sclerae or teeth.2 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation presents as blue-hued pigmentation of the skin that may also involve the sclerae, nails, teeth, and oral mucosa. The reported incidence varies from 2% to 15% in patients treated for acne to 41% to 54% in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and orthopedic infections, respectively.4-6 Although minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation is a clinical diagnosis, skin biopsy can confirm the diagnosis and reveals subepidermal deposition of granular black pigment both interstitially and intracellularly (Figure 2). The pigment reacts positively with staining techniques used to detect iron and/or melanin (Perl’s Prussian blue and Fontana-Masson, respectively). In contrast, ecchymoses stain positive for iron only. While the mechanism of hyperpigmentation remains unclear, histopathologic studies indicate that minocycline and/or its metabolites likely form insoluble complexes with iron that deposit in tissue.7 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation is classified into 3 types based on clinical findings and histologic staining, though these categories may overlap. In type I, blue pigmentation is found in scars, commonly facial acne scars, and stains positive for iron only. In type II, blue pigmentation affects normal skin, typically on the extremities, and stains positive for both iron and melanin. Type III presents with muddy brown discoloration most prominent in sun-exposed skin and stains positive for melanin.8 This patient’s presentation was consistent with type II hyperpigmentation and notable for both the striking degree of pigmentation and for its rapid development after only 6 months of treatment. Most minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation occurs after a year, though small case series have reported pigmentation after only a few weeks.5,6,9Several characteristics of this patient may have contributed to the more rapid onset, including the longstanding purpura on his arms, which increases dermal iron available for chelation, as well as hepatic and kidney disease, which impair drug metabolism and excretion. Minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation persists after drug cessation and is challenging to treat. Given the small size of the pigment particle, treatment is best approached with picosecond or Q-switched lasers.10In addition to its effects on skin pigmentation, minocycline use in children can result in permanent teeth discoloration and bone hypoplasia and should be avoided during pregnancy and in children younger than 8 years old.2 Minocycline was discontinued and daptomycin was started in its place. The patient declined treatment for the pigmentation changes because they were not bothersome to him.
